summary: Research-led UX design for Chicago fintech, insurance, logistics and B2B SaaS teams.
abstract: We are a remote-first UX design agency headquartered in Reston, Virginia, working with Chicago product teams on user research, interface design, prototyping and usability testing. Chicago engagements focus on dense, data-heavy software: order entry, claims, dispatch and analytics. Projects start at $5,000 for a UX audit, and our Eastern Time base sits one hour ahead of Chicago, so almost the whole workday is shared.

sections.h2: Why do Chicago product teams bring in an outside UX design agency?
sections.answer: Chicago product teams bring in a UX design agency when complex workflows, such as trade entry, claims handling or shipment tracking, cost users time and the in-house design bench is too thin to fix them quickly. An agency adds researchers and designers for a defined scope, then hands the work back to your team.
sections.body: Much of the software built in Chicago is operational: traders watching prices tick, adjusters moving a claim through review, dispatchers rerouting loads around a rail delay. These users repeat the same tasks all day and notice every extra click. A UX design agency Chicago teams can lean on studies those routines first, then redesigns the screens around them. The full scope is on our digital product design services page. We do not have a Chicago office, and we say so up front: the team works remotely and travels for workshops when a project needs a room.

sections.h2: Which Chicago industries shape our UX work?
sections.answer: Four Chicago industries account for most of the product types we design for: trading and fintech, insurance, logistics and freight, and B2B SaaS.
items: Trading and fintech, from derivatives and options platforms to wealth and payments apps, where real-time data, risk warnings and order confirmation must be unambiguous (Finance UI UX design).
Insurance carriers and insurtech, including agent portals, quote-and-bind flows, policy servicing and first-notice-of-loss forms that policyholders finish on a phone.
Logistics and freight technology, shaped by Chicago's role as the country's rail and trucking crossroads: load boards, visibility dashboards and yard tools (Supply chain UI UX design).
B2B SaaS companies around the Loop and Fulton Market that need onboarding, admin settings and reporting to scale with larger accounts (SaaS UI UX design).
Early-stage startups coming out of the city's incubators and accelerators that need a testable MVP before a seed or Series A raise (Startups UI UX design).

sections.h2: What a Chicago UX engagement delivers
sections.answer: A typical Chicago UX engagement delivers six outputs: workflow research, an expert audit, an information architecture, high-fidelity UI, a component library and tested prototypes.

items.title: Workflow research.
items.body: Shadowing and interviews with 5–12 people per role, for example underwriters and independent agents using the same quoting tool.

items.title: Expert UX audit.
items.body: A heuristic and WCAG 2.2 review of the flows that matter most, for example an order ticket and its confirmation screen.

items.title: Information architecture.
items.body: Card sorting and tree testing to restructure navigation, for example a carrier portal that grew one menu item per release.

items.title: High-fidelity UI.
items.body: Figma screens for desktop and mobile with dense tables, filters and alerts designed for scanning rather than reading.

items.title: Component library.
items.body: Tokens, components and usage notes that let several squads ship screens that look and behave alike.

items.title: Tested prototypes.
items.body: Clickable prototypes validated with five participants per round before engineering commits sprint capacity.

sections.h2: Our five-stage process for Chicago clients
sections.answer: Most Chicago projects run 4–8 weeks across five stages, starting with a scoping call and ending with a developer handoff your engineers can build from.

items.title: Scoping call (1–2 days)
items.body: We map the users, the workflow under pressure and the metric you want to move, then confirm budget and dates in writing.

items.title: Field research (5–10 days)
items.body: Researchers observe real sessions, for example a dispatcher's shift or a trader's market open, and review analytics and support tickets.

items.title: Alignment workshop (2–3 days)
items.body: Product, engineering and compliance agree on priorities in remote sessions on Central Time; we travel to Chicago for in-person workshops when the scope justifies it.

items.title: Design sprints (10–20 days)
items.body: Designers build flows, UI and a working prototype, with two review sessions a week so stakeholders steer early.

items.title: Validation and handoff (5–10 days)
items.body: We run usability rounds, fix what fails, and deliver annotated specs and components to your developers.

sections.h2: Agency sprint or a full-time Chicago design hire?
sections.answer: An agency sprint suits a defined problem with a deadline, while a full-time hire suits a permanent, ongoing design need. Many Chicago teams use a sprint first to prove the value of design, then hire.

sections.h2: What does a UX design agency Chicago engagement cost?
sections.answer: A UX design agency Chicago engagement costs $5,000–$15,000 for a 2–3 week audit and $25,000–$60,000 for a 4–8 week research and design sprint. Scope drives the price: how many workflows, how many user roles, how much research and whether a component library is included.
sections.body: End-to-end product design with a design system runs $60,000–$180,000 over 8–16 weeks. Teams that want a designer embedded in their squads month to month pay $15,000–$40,000 per month. Each proposal is fixed-scope, so the figure you approve is the figure you pay. If your product is a trading or analytics tool, see how we approached a similar problem in our trading journal case study, and for warehouse and freight workflows, the warehouse error-resolution case study.

sections.h2: What changes for users after a Chicago UX redesign
sections.answer: A research-led redesign changes four things for Chicago users and the teams behind them: fewer errors in high-stakes tasks, faster task completion, quicker onboarding and a consistent interface across products.

items.title: Fewer high-stakes errors
items.body: Clear confirmations, sensible defaults and readable states reduce mistakes such as a wrong order size or a misfiled claim.

items.title: Faster repeat tasks
items.body: Keyboard paths, saved views and tighter layouts cut the seconds that add up across a full trading day or dispatch shift.

items.title: Quicker onboarding
items.body: New agents, brokers and admins reach competence sooner when navigation follows the way they already think about the work.

items.title: One consistent interface
items.body: A shared design system keeps legacy modules and new features aligned.

sections.answer: Five questions Chicago teams raise most often before they sign with a UX design agency.

faqs.q: Is your team based in Chicago?
faqs.a: No. We are a remote-first UX design agency headquartered in Reston, Virginia. Our Eastern Time hours overlap almost entirely with Chicago's Central Time, and we travel for on-site workshops when a project calls for it.

faqs.q: Can you design for regulated trading and insurance products?
faqs.a: Yes. We design within your compliance requirements, involve your legal and risk reviewers in workshops, and document disclosures, warnings and audit-relevant states in the handoff.

faqs.q: How do you research users who are too busy for interviews?
faqs.a: We use short contextual observation, screen recordings with consent and unmoderated tests that fit around shifts, so traders, adjusters and dispatchers give 20–30 minutes instead of an hour.

faqs.q: When can a Chicago project begin?
faqs.a: A UX design agency Chicago teams sign with today can usually start 1–2 weeks after the scoping call, once the proposal is approved.

faqs.q: Do you work with our developers after handoff?
faqs.a: Yes. Designers stay available for implementation questions and design QA during the build, and documentation lives in Figma and Storybook.
